title: Jangjorim
subtitle: Soy-braised beef with hard-boiled eggs
excerpt: Chunks of beef are simmered low and slow in a sweet soy broth until deeply flavoured, then joined by peeled hard-boiled eggs that absorb the same braising liquid. Jangjorim is a long-keeping banchan designed to be made in a batch and eaten over several days. It takes around 50 minutes and serves 4 alongside rice.
sourceNotes: Jangjorim is one of Korea's traditional preserved banchan, developed in the era before refrigeration when soy-braised foods could be kept for extended periods. The high soy content acts as a preservative, and the dish was made in larger quantities than needed for a single meal. It remains a practical household staple today.

recipe.batchNotes: Keeps well in the fridge for up to 5 days. Flavour deepens over time. Make a larger batch and eat throughout the week.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made a day ahead. The beef and eggs absorb more flavour as they sit in the cooled braising liquid overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: Jangjorim is a Korean preserved banchan made by braising beef or other proteins in a concentrated soy, sugar and garlic broth until the liquid reduces to a thick, dark glaze. The high soy content keeps the dish for several days in the fridge. The name comes from 'jang' meaning soy sauce and 'jorim' meaning to reduce or braise.

Banchan are the small side dishes served alongside rice at a Korean meal. They sit in the centre of the table for everyone to share and typically include a combination of vegetable, egg, tofu and meat preparations. Some banchan are eaten immediately while others, like jangjorim, are made in batches and kept in the fridge for several days.

content.text: side and takes about 50 minutes in total, most of which is hands-off simmering time.
is one of those dishes that rewards making ahead: the beef and eggs become more deeply flavoured the longer they sit in the braising liquid.

Use a saucepan that fits the beef in a reasonably snug layer. If the pan is too wide, the liquid spreads thin and reduces too fast before the beef has time to become tender. A medium saucepan works well for this quantity.
Place the beef chunks in a medium saucepan. Cover with cold water and bring to the boil. Boil for 3 minutes, then drain and rinse. This removes impurities and keeps the braising broth clean.
Return the blanched beef to the pan. Add the soy sauce, sugar, garlic cloves, gochugaru if using, and the 300ml of water.
Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat to low. Simmer with the lid on for 20 minutes, turning the beef occasionally.

Add the peeled hard-boiled eggs to the pan. Simmer uncovered for a further 15 to 20 minutes, turning the eggs regularly, until the braising liquid reduces to a thick, dark glaze and the eggs have taken on colour all over.
Remove from the heat and drizzle with sesame oil. Allow to cool slightly before serving. The beef can be pulled apart into smaller shreds with two forks before serving if preferred.

items.symptom: Braising liquid reduces too quickly and catches on the bottom
items.cause: The heat was too high during the uncovered reduction stage
items.fix: Keep the heat at low to medium-low once the lid comes off. Stir and check every few minutes. If the liquid is almost gone but the beef is not tender, add a splash of water and continue.

items.symptom: Eggs look pale and barely coloured after cooking
items.cause: The eggs were added too late and there was not enough soy liquid left to colour them
items.fix: Add the eggs earlier in the process while there is still plenty of braising liquid. Turn them every 5 minutes so all sides take on colour evenly.

items.symptom: Beef is tough and chewy rather than tender
items.cause: The beef was cut into pieces that were too large, or the simmer was not long enough
items.fix: Sirloin becomes tender with time. If the beef is still tough at 35 minutes, add a little more water and continue simmering with the lid on until it gives easily.

content.text: Jangjorim is the kind of banchan that Korean mothers and grandmothers make on a Sunday so there is something ready in the fridge all week. A spoonful of the shredded beef and a halved egg alongside a bowl of rice is a complete quick meal. The dish is intensely savoury and is always eaten in small amounts with plenty of plain rice to balance the seasoning.
